storyboard.claim: Consent and arousal feel like they should be the same signal, but biologically they are not.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery, tense, caught between what her mind wants and what her body is doing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the moral-expectation setup from the prior beat with the biological claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names that this is a biological split, not a moral one, before the mechanism is explained.

storyboard.claim: Arousal is a physiological response, not a conscious green light, and the mechanism starts with extreme terror.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery holding still, body reacting before her mind can weigh in.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Unpacks 'distinct processes' into the specific claim: arousal is body, not permission.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: mostly restates the narration's own framing before the nervous-system detail lands.

storyboard.claim: In extreme terror the sympathetic nervous system fires and the body preps for fight or flight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A jolt through Avery's body as her nervous system activates.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the abstract claim to the actual nervous-system trigger.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the activation a felt jolt rather than a textbook phrase.

storyboard.claim: Adrenaline, noradrenaline and cortisol flood the body; heart rate spikes, blood vessels dilate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery's body under a flood of stress hormones — visibly keyed up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the first physical symptoms of the fight-or-flight state just named.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: itemizes symptoms the narration already lists explicitly.

storyboard.claim: Breath quickens, pupils dilate, blood is redirected — the exact same symptoms as sexual arousal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery's surprised realization as fear-symptoms and arousal-symptoms turn out identical.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pivot: the symptom list from the last two beats turns out to double as arousal's own list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Flags this as the beat's actual reveal, not just another symptom.

storyboard.claim: Fear and lust are systemically identical — the body cannot tell a racing heart from terror apart from a racing heart from lust.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two rhythms — fear and lust — tracing the exact same waveform.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the prior beat's 'exact same symptoms' claim into the structural diagram.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the two states as literally synchronized signals, not just a verbal comparison.

storyboard.claim: The body doesn't know the difference — it just registers that it's highly stimulated.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery, overloaded, no longer able to name what she's feeling.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the matchWave point with the plain-language summary line.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: restates the diagram's point in words rather than adding new content.

storyboard.claim: The 1974 Dutton and Aaron shaky bridge experiment: an attractive researcher approached men on a bridge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A man crossing an unsteady high bridge, approached mid-crossing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings in outside evidence for the fear/arousal overlap just established.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grounds the abstract claim in a named, dated real study.

storyboard.claim: Men on the terrifying swaying bridge, versus a solid one, were far more likely to call the researcher afterward.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same man, visibly rattled, still shaken from the crossing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the experiment's actual result after the setup.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the surprising outcome — fear predicted later contact, not comfort.

storyboard.claim: The result is explained by misattribution of arousal: fear-induced adrenaline from the scary bridge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The man, still flooded with adrenaline, unaware of its true source.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the psychological mechanism behind the surprising call-back result.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the phenomenon its technical name before applying it to Gray.

storyboard.claim: Their brains misread the physiological fear response as intense sexual attraction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The man's confused double-take, mistaking his own fear signal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies exactly what the brain misattributes fear to.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: restates the mechanism from the previous beat with a sharper label.

storyboard.claim: The brain tricks itself into reading a pounding heart as arousal — and Gray is doing exactly this to Avery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray reaching toward a tense Avery, applying the bridge-experiment mechanism in person.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Snaps the outside research straight back onto the book's own relationship.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns an abstract psychology finding into a specific, named act by Gray.

storyboard.claim: Gray hijacks her terror-induced adrenaline spike and cross-wires it directly with sexual arousal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A jolt running through Avery's body under Gray's control, rerouted rather than felt cleanly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the exact mechanism Gray is running on Avery's nervous system.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the hijack visible as a rerouted jolt, not just a verbal claim.

storyboard.claim: He weaponizes her own anatomy against her logical mind — a total hostile takeover of her biology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray controlling Avery's reactions like strings, her body no longer her own to direct.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalates the cross-wiring claim into full control of her body.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames it as total control, not just a single misfired signal.

storyboard.claim: Macca forces the reader to sit inside the agonizing gap between what the body does and what the mind desires.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A visible split running through Avery — body pulling one way, mind another.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the emotional cost of the hostile takeover just described.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the internal split a visible fracture rather than an abstract phrase.

storyboard.claim: It's a brave authorial choice: Avery's mind wants safety.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery pulling inward, seeking safety with her mind alone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the mind's half of the gap just diagrammed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Isolates the mind's want before the body's betrayal is shown next.

storyboard.claim: She wants to be far from the bloodied shiv, but her body stretches and reacts, completely betraying her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery's body reaching toward what her mind is recoiling from.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the body's half of the gap, contradicting the mind's want from the prior beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the betrayal as a physical reach, the opposite of what her mind wants.

storyboard.claim: Macca refuses a clean ending — Avery never has the scene where she realizes it's a mistake and bravely pulls away.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery staying put, not pulling back, refusing the tidy exit the narration rejects.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what does NOT happen, staged as absence rather than the rejected resolution.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks this as a refused outcome, not a real story beat.

storyboard.claim: Nor does Gray become a gentle romance hero — the discomfort isn't a flaw, the discomfort is the text.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray, unmoved and unsoftened, exactly as controlled and dangerous as before.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pairs with the prior beat's refusal: neither character gets the genre's usual resolution.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the essay's thesis line directly, not just the negated cliche.

storyboard.claim: It isn't just Avery whose nervous system is being hijacked — the argument is about to widen.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery still caught in her own reaction, on the edge of the scene that reframes her as an example.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Signals the turn from Avery's body to the reader's, before the reader is named.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: a pure transition line flagging a widening argument, no new claim yet.

storyboard.claim: Macca is doing the exact same thing to the person holding the physical book — to you, the reader.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A reader-stand-in caught holding the very book being discussed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the 'meta' turn promised in the previous beat by naming the reader directly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts a concrete figure on screen for 'the reader' instead of leaving it abstract.

storyboard.claim: The structure of the narrative itself is designed to mirror the chemical reaction happening inside Avery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mirror shows Avery on one side and the reader on the other — both experiencing the same chemical spike, the narrative designed to sync them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes literal the claim that the reader and Avery run the same reaction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the abstract 'mirrors' claim a literal reflecting image.

storyboard.claim: The trigger warnings at the book's opening don't just clinically list themes — they boldly state something else.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in reading a printed page of warnings, about to be surprised by its tone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves the mirror claim into concrete evidence: the book's own opening page.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the specific text that follows as evidence, not just a claim.

storyboard.claim: The trigger warning itself, quoted: an invitation into 'unhinged, depraved darkness.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in reacting to the book's own provocative language.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quotes the actual line the previous beat set up.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the book's own words rather than a paraphrase.

storyboard.claim: That's an explicit invitation — the author is literally telling the reader what's coming.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in, addressed head-on rather than reading privately.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the quoted line as a direct address rather than mere warning.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes the trigger warning as an invitation, not a disclaimer.

storyboard.claim: The author wants the reader's consent because the prose is calibrated to run the same intermittent reinforcement loop as the protagonist's.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Skinner box mechanism, its lever and pellet dispenser standing in for the reader's own experience.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the exact mechanism the invitation is actually asking the reader to enter.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the book's central experimental metaphor by name, applied directly to the reader.

storyboard.claim: You're in the Skinner box too, right alongside the protagonist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in inside the same box mechanism just described.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirms the mechanism named in the previous beat applies to the reader specifically.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: restates the previous beat's claim as direct address.

storyboard.claim: When Gray calls himself demon boy and cracks a witty joke, the reader gets a dopamine hit of charm.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray, charming and self-aware, delivering the joke straight to the audience.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the first concrete example of the reinforcement loop just named: a reward.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the specific reward (charm/humor) rather than the mechanism in the abstract.

storyboard.claim: The reader becomes invested in Gray being good — then when he threatens to destroy someone, the reader's own pulse spikes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in tensing at the threat, invested despite knowing better.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the punishment/threat half of the loop, following the reward beat before it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the loop's variable-ratio swing: reward, then threat, on the same reader.

storyboard.claim: Reflect on the scene where Gray defends Avery from Sam.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray squaring off against Sam, the confrontation about to begin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the specific scene the reader is asked to recall as a worked example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the scene and both characters before the specific actions are shown.

storyboard.claim: Gray slams his fist into the wall, demands to know where her boyfriend is — violently possessive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray lunging, fist near the wall, demanding answers from Sam.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the concrete action of the scene just set up.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the specific violent act rather than summarizing it as 'a confrontation.'

storyboard.claim: Reading it, you are internally cheering for Gray — wanting him to beat Sam up and protect her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in genuinely cheering the violence just witnessed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the reader's actual reaction to the violent scene just staged.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the reader's real, uncomfortable response rather than the scene's content again.

storyboard.claim: Even so, he is objectively a monster — he is the villain, and the fourth wall isn't a window here.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The monster beneath Gray's charm, visible for a moment underneath him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Corrects the cheering from the previous beat with the plain moral fact.
storyboard.addedInformation: Surfaces what the reader's cheering was obscuring: the villain underneath.

storyboard.claim: The fourth wall is a mirror reflecting the reader's own reactions back, forcing an uncomfortable recognition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in facing their own reflection instead of the story.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mechanism (mirror, not window) behind the discomfort just revealed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the reader the actual subject of the reflection, not the story.

storyboard.claim: By the midpoint, judging Avery for letting a man with a knife touch her means hypocritically judging your own reading pleasure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in caught mid-read, unable to separate judgment of Avery from judgment of themselves.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the mirror claim into its practical consequence: you can no longer judge her cleanly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Spells out the specific hypocrisy the mirror produces.

storyboard.claim: You are the one turning the pages, seeking the same dopamine hit she is — the genre's most subversive move.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in still turning pages, chasing the same reward Avery chases.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the reader's own compulsion in the same terms used for Avery's loop earlier.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the reader's page-turning directly back to the reinforcement mechanism, not just empathy.

storyboard.claim: In real time, the author proves how easily our own biology can be manipulated by pacing and variable reinforcement.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in's reactions pulled by unseen strings from the pacing of the prose.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the reader's own compulsion into the essay's demonstrated proof.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names narrative pacing itself as the controlling hand, not just the content.

storyboard.claim: We like to think we're rational, but Macca proves we're just as susceptible to the slot machine as Avery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in pulling the lever of the same slot machine trapping Avery.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the human-scale version of the Skinner box the reader has just been shown to be inside.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the manipulation claim its second, plainer-language metaphor.

storyboard.claim: The next question: how does Gray sustain the illusion, keeping both Avery and the reader on his side over time?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's composed public face, the illusion he maintains for everyone watching.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from 'we are susceptible' to the mechanics of how Gray keeps it running.
storyboard.addedInformation: Poses the maintenance question the next section will answer.

storyboard.claim: You'd expect the hornet stings to outweigh the candy bars, but Gray uses cognitive reframing to keep the balance tipped his way.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A scale weighing the relationship's cruelty against its rewards, still tipped toward the rewards.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the maintenance question with the actual mechanism: reframing the balance itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows numerically why the abuse doesn't outweigh the reward in Avery's (and the reader's) experience.
